'''''Salix triandra''''', with the common names '''almond willow''', '''almond-leaved willow''' or '''black maul willow''', is a species of [[willow]] native to [[Europe]] and [[Western Asia|Western]] and [[Central Asia]]. It is found from south-eastern [[England]] east to [[Lake Baikal]], and south to [[Spain]] and the [[Mediterranean]] east to the [[Caucasus]], and the [[Alborz]] Mountains. It usually grows in [[riparian zone|riparian habitat]]s, on river and [[stream]] banks, and in [[wetland]]s.<ref name=rdm>Meikle, R. D. (1984). ''Willows and Poplars of Great Britain and Ireland''. BSBI Handbook No. 4. {{ISBN|0-901158-07-0}}.</ref><ref name=rushforth>Rushforth, K. (1999). ''Trees of Britain and Europe''. Collins {{ISBN|0-00-220013-9}}.</ref><ref name=dvf>Den Virtuella Floran: [http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/salica/salix/salitri.html ''Salix triandra'' (in Swedish; with maps)]</ref>

==Description==
''Salix triandra'' is a [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] growing to {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, usually multistemmed, with an irregular, often leaning crown. Young [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is smooth grey-brown, becoming scaly on older stems with large scales exfoliating (like a [[Platanus|plane]] tree) to leave orange-brown patches. The [[leaf|leaves]] are broad, lanceolate, 4–11 cm long and 1–3 cm wide, with a serrated margin; they are dull dark green above and green to glaucous-green below, with a 1–2-cm [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] with two conspicuous basal [[stipule]]s.

The [[flower]]s are produced in [[catkin]]s in early spring at the same time as the new leaves, and pollinated by [[insect]]s. They are [[plant sexuality|dioecious]], with male and female catkins on separate trees; the male catkins are 2.5–8 cm long, the female catkins 2–4 cm long. The male flowers have three [[stamen]]s, a useful identification feature with most other willows having two or five stamens.<ref name=rdm/><ref name=rushforth/>

==Taxonomy==
The scientific name derives from the male flowers having three stamens. The English common name refers to the similarity in leaf shape to [[almond]] leaves.

The [[variety (botany)|variety]] ''Salix triandra'' var. ''hoffmanniana'' Bab., found in [[Great Britain]], is distinguished by being smaller (rarely over {{convert|4|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall) and densely branched, with smaller leaves 2–7 cm long and 1–2.5 cm wide not glaucous below. It is not considered distinct by all authorities, particularly on continental Europe, so its range outside Britain, if any, is not reported.<ref name=rdm/>

''Salix triandra'' readily forms natural [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] with ''[[Salix viminalis]]'', the hybrid being named ''Salix × mollissima'' Hoffm. ex Elwert.<ref name=rdm/>

Plants from [[Eastern Asia]], formerly treated as ''S. triandra'' var. ''nipponica'' (Franch. & Savatier) Seem.,<ref name=dvf/> are now considered the distinct species ''[[Salix nipponica]]''. They share the feature of male flowers with three stamens.<ref name=foc>Flora of China: [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=210001955 ''Salix nipponica'']</ref>

==Cultivation and uses==
The plant is a potential [[biomass]] source for [[biofuel]] energy generation.<ref name=npgs>{{GRIN | accessdate=2013-01-13}}</ref>

In the Russian honey industry, the plant is used as a [[nectar]] source for [[honeybee]]s.<ref name=npgs/>

;Basket weaving
The shoots ([[withy|withies]]) are extensively used for [[Basket weaving|basketmaking]]. It is one of the most important willows for this purpose after ''[[Salix viminalis]]'', with several selected [[cultivar]]s including: 'Black Maul', 'Grizette', 'Mottled Spaniards', 'Sarda', and 'Yellow Dutch'.<ref name=rdm/>

Woven withies have been used in the creation of the large outdoor sculpture "[[Willow Man]]", located near [[Bridgwater]] in [[England]].
